summary: Three-lens review of the revised LangChain adapter spike S2b (concurrency, outcome attribution, evidence), then adversarial verification of each finding

sound.checked_and_sound: Dispatch: create_agent 1.4.9 issues one Send per pending tool call (factory.py:2032) and Pregel runs each as a thread-pool task (_runner.py:258-275), so on every non-failing path the turnstile does give index order; my control (10 calls on 6 workers, 30/30 identical) and the retry case (k0,k0,k1,k2 with the retry inside the region) confirm the spike's check 6 for that path. A second model turn reusing the same call ids is fine (probe: two turns of c0..c2 ran k0,k1,k2,k0,k1,k2), because SerialOrder.after_model runs last of all after_model hooks (factory.py:1857-1867) and resets indices under the lock after the previous step's tasks have finished. No hang arises from a validation failure mid-message (ToolInvocationError is raised inside the try; probe gave success/error/success in order), from duplicate or missing ids (rejected in after_model before any dispatch), from a call id not in the current message (rejected before the wait, and nobody waits on it), or from ToolCallLimitMiddleware injecting ToolMessages (loud reject 'non-AI model response', no hang); every exception type including BaseException passes through the finally. BudgetExceeded raised mid-message is deterministic in the recorded events (300/300 at 5 calls, 20/20 at 10 calls on 6 workers) because a post-exhaustion ToolBox.call emits nothing (toolbox.py:181-184), though the hang mechanism of finding 1 applies to it too. The design does assume thread dispatch: it also works for a sequential dispatcher only if that dispatcher delivers in index order, and a sync Condition wait would block an event loop, but the async path is rejected up front in abefore_agent/awrap_tool_call, which matches the spike's check 7. The ToolBox is not thread-safe, so serialisation is required rather than optional; what the product must add is an abort flag, a wait timeout that latches harness ERROR, re-entry detection and adapter-owned middleware composition, as detailed in the findings. All probes ran in memory against the installed versions; I briefly created one helper file in the session scratchpad (outside the repository), deleted it, and wrote nothing into the repository.

Latest run is out/run-0005 (same source hashes as run-0004; FINDINGS cites 0003/0004), 17 OK and 1 FAIL. (1) The brief's demand was wrong for injected faults: Perturbation.before short-circuits the real tool (interfaces.py:122-123, toolbox.py:274-286) and ToolFault is the frozen exception for real and injected failures, so body counts of native minus one and ToolFault instead of ValueError are correct, and the spike was right not to run the body to equalise; the gap matters only through exception type (finding 1). Parity that holds in parity.json: none = no answer on both sides, adapter FAIL/crash with 1 boundary call; retry = 'forty-two' on both, adapter PASS with 2 boundary calls; error = 'unavailable' with an identical error observation, adapter FAIL/completed with 1 call; real-error-retry = PASS, 2 bodies, 2 calls, matching native's 2 bodies. What does not hold: exception type in the no-middleware case and body counts in all three (1/0, 2/1, 1/0). (2) With default settings both middlewares catch ToolFault like any Exception (default_retry_on, _retry.py:70-76), so retry and handling behave as native except for the exhaustion text; budget and replay-miss exceptions swallowed by them stay correctly classified because the latches are set before they propagate. (3) reject_unsupported is compatible with the frozen protocol and acceptance tests and is the right change for async and replay; live in-body cases need no kernel change (finding 3). (4) Model-visible success and validation text is byte-identical to native on 1.4.9/1.7.7/1.1.1, SerialOrder's finally-release and index ordering are sound, and the replay final-answer limit is stated accurately.

I read run_spike.py, all spike sources, FINDINGS.md, the run-0005 evidence and the installed LangChain source, and ran read-only in-memory probes; I did not run run_spike.py. Of the 18 checks, ten test behaviour and could fail if it were absent (experiment, native_parity, exception_positions, exactly_once, argument_validation, built_in_faults, budget, multi_call, unsupported_shapes, message_shapes: nine OK, one FAIL); two pass by asserting that a defect is still present (unsupported_replay_limit requires FAIL/crash at run_spike.py:422-428, replay_answer_limit requires REPRODUCED for an altered answer at :487), which FINDINGS.md:21 does disclose, so the result to carry is 15 OK, 2 known limits, 1 FAIL rather than 17 OK; six are bookkeeping, of which user_burden cannot fail and cost has no time threshold. The multi-call check is real and discriminating: each of the 20 repetitions is run_trial in a fresh worker process (same spec and seed, so repetitions rather than distinct trials), it compares full (kind, payload) event sequences and seals, and when I removed the gate in memory the call order reversed in 5 of 20 runs. The native side of the parity checks is genuinely native (create_agent with no ARCI middleware, run_spike.py:62-85), and argument-validation feedback is identical to native in all three policies, though the code comment at arci_langchain.py:179 is wrong that native validates outside user middleware (tool_node.py:966-981 validates inside execute). Cost: within a run the 12 samples sit within about 3 percent of the median, but run medians with identical sources were 5.63, 0.92, 1.00 and 1.06 s (1.57 s on the earlier source); it is parent-side wall time around worker start, LangChain import and grading for a trivial scripted trial at one worker, so the plan should carry 'about 1 s fixed overhead per trial on an idle machine, budget 1.5 s, 5.6 s seen under load' and no speed-up claim over S2, which FINDINGS.md:23-26 states fairly. The replay-answer limit and the unsupported-in-replay limit are stated plainly and not understated. On the API question: nothing in LangChain prevents a helper that builds the full list; one middleware object cannot be both outermost and innermost, but one outermost middleware plus proxy tools gave the same guarantees in my probe. Minimal honest description of what a user writes today: a tool factory make_tools(task, seed) that is safe to call again with seed 0 in replay; one builder function per arm that wraps their create_agent call, uses the tools handed in and places their middleware between the two ARCI entries; one glue line; a check function, in a LangChain-free module if they want the measured cost; and arci.yaml with the task, five dotted references, fault conditions naming their tools, and budgets; plus, not yet in the spike, a way to turn a task into the agent's input.

surviving.title: A fatal exception in one call of a multi-call message makes the recorded trace nondeterministic and can deadlock the turnstile
surviving.claim: The turnstile assumes every indexed call arrives, but when one call raises out of the region LangGraph cancels the not-yet-started sibling futures in arbitrary set order while the started ones keep running. The calls that still reach ToolBox after the failure therefore vary from run to run (different tool_start events, body executions and sealed hashes), and if a cancelled index sits below a started one the started thread waits forever and graph.invoke never returns. FINDINGS.md lines 41-44 and check 5/6 claim the finally-release and determinism in general, but the evidence is only 2-call messages (scripted_model.py:39) on the success path or with a budget fault.
surviving.recommendation: Product SerialOrder must (1) keep an aborted flag: when any exception other than the ToolInvocationError that ToolNode converts leaves the region, set it under the condition and notify_all, and every later index raises a fixed exception without calling ToolBox, so the recorded trace always ends at the failing call regardless of which threads started; (2) put a timeout on wait_for and turn expiry into a harness ERROR through a real harness latch, never FAIL/timeout; (3) decide unknown-tool calls deliberately (pass them to ToolBox, which already returns unknown_tool as a ToolFault, toolbox.py:289-296) rather than raising a fatal reject. Acceptance test: at least 1000 repetitions with more calls than pool threads (set max_concurrency) and the failure at index 0 and mid-message, requiring one sealed hash and zero hangs.

surviving.title: Middleware placement is trusted, not enforced: a retry outside SerialOrder deadlocks every retried call, and anything after Boundary is silently dropped
surviving.claim: The adapter hands [SerialOrder, Boundary] to the user's builder and relies on the user splicing their middleware between the two. If a retrying middleware ends up before SerialOrder, the second attempt re-enters the turnstile with an index that has already been released and waits forever, even for a single-call message. If user middleware ends up after Boundary it never runs, because Boundary discards its handler. Neither case sets adapter_error, so ARCI seals an ordinary agent failure.
surviving.recommendation: The product adapter should own composition: take the user's middleware list (or a builder that returns it) and assemble [SerialOrder, *user, Boundary] itself instead of asking users to splice. Independently, SerialOrder must detect re-entry of an already-consumed call id and raise a harness ERROR with a fixed diagnostic naming the ordering rule, and the wait must have a timeout that latches harness ERROR. Add a build-time or first-call check that Boundary is innermost (for example a sentinel the adapter can observe when the handler passed to Boundary is not ToolNode's execute), and tests for both misplacements.

surviving.title: The turn is held across retry backoff, so wall time scales with the number of parallel calls, and BudgetExceeded is itself retried with sleeps
surviving.claim: Because the whole user chain including ToolRetryMiddleware runs inside the turn, backoff sleeps that are concurrent natively become sequential, multiplying wall time by the number of calls in the message. ARCI's own BudgetExceeded is an Exception, so the default retry policy retries it with full backoff for every remaining call and then converts it into a ToolMessage. Every spike fixture uses initial_delay=0, jitter=False and at most 2 calls, so neither the cost figure nor the budget check exercises this.
surviving.recommendation: State serialisation as a measured-time limit of the adapter and give max_seconds guidance (worst case = calls per message x per-call retry time), or exclude wall-clock comparisons for multi-call messages. Make budget exhaustion and adapter rejections non-retryable inside the region: Boundary should surface them through a carrier that user retry/error middleware cannot catch (for example a BaseException-derived signal that SerialOrder converts back to the original exception outside the user chain), so no backoff is slept after the budget is gone and the trial ends at the exhausting call. Add a check with non-zero delays and three or more calls.

surviving.title: Exception identity is erased for real and injected failures, so type-filtered retry/error policies diverge from the deployed agent and are graded FAIL, not ERROR
surviving.claim: Every tool failure reaches user middleware as arci ToolFault. With type-blind settings behaviour matches native, but with a type filter (the idiom in every LangChain docstring example for both middlewares) the adapter changes the outcome even with NO fault injected, and an injected timeout never exercises the user's TimeoutError path. The result is FAIL/crash counted against the agent, in both arms, which can hide a real regression or block a sound candidate. FINDINGS.md mentions this in one sentence (lines 103-108) and omits it from 'Supported scope and risks'; no check covers it, and it contradicts design rule 4 (unsupported => ERROR, never FAIL).
surviving.recommendation: Give this a design answer before phase 3, not a doc note. Live: have DerivedToolSet.execute stash the original exception and have Boundary re-raise that object (ToolFault as __cause__) for non-injected failures, so the gate's trials are faithful. Injected faults: let the user map fault kind to an exception factory (e.g. {'timeout': TimeoutError}), default ToolFault. Replay cannot re-raise the original (worker.py:125-127 gives no tools), so apply the same mapping to the recorded 'TypeName: message' detail and end as ERROR when a recorded real failure's type is undeclared; the rule must be identical live and in replay or fingerprints and call counts diverge. Add parity checks for retry_on=(TimeoutError,), an isinstance ToolErrorMiddleware, and default on_failure='continue' text.
surviving.corrected_claim:
Every tool failure, real or injected, reaches user middleware as arci ToolFault (toolbox.py:298-307, 254-255). With type-blind policies (default retry_on, handlers that ignore the exception) the adapter matches native. With a type-sensitive policy it diverges, even when no fault is injected: retry_on=(TimeoutError,) does not retry a real TimeoutError (native: 2 bodies, answer 'forty-two'; adapter: 1 body, ToolFault raised), an isinstance(exc, ValueError) ToolErrorMiddleware handler does not handle a real ValueError, and an injected tool_timeout never reaches a TimeoutError path. Default on_failure='continue' text also changes to 'ToolFault: error: TimeoutError: ...' with numbers normalised. The uncaught ToolFault is graded FAIL/crash, not ERROR (worker.py ToolFault branch, runner.py:206-208, harness latch unset).

Type filters appear in two of ToolRetryMiddleware's seven docstring examples and in ToolErrorMiddleware's only example, not in every example. FINDINGS.md does disclose the limit (lines 103-108, and the Decision headline for the injected case), but understates it: it does not say the result is an agent FAIL on non-injected trials, omits it from 'Supported scope and risks', and no check or fixture uses a type filter (user_app.py:34, probe_app.py:57-60).

It is not a literal breach of brief rule 4, which lists async, artifacts, return_direct and Command; brief rule 2 and frozen interfaces.py:47-52 prescribe ToolFault and FAIL, and the adapter cannot see user middleware to detect a type filter. It is a fidelity gap that needs a design answer before phase 3. Any fix must raise the same exception type and message live and in replay: replay has no tool objects (worker.py:125-127) and only the normalised, unqualified 'TypeName: message' is recorded, so re-raising the raw original object live would still differ from replay in model-visible text.

surviving.title: Private-API validation and formatting span three independently versioned packages, misplace validation relative to user middleware, and are avoidable with public APIs
surviving.claim: The adapter imports langchain_core's private _format_output and langgraph-prebuilt's unexported ToolInvocationError; neither package is bounded by the planned langchain>=1.4,<2 pin. A drift fails inside the user's retry/error scope after the body has already run, so it surfaces as agent FAILs rather than ERROR. The pre-validation in SerialOrder is also not where native validates: the comment 'as native ToolNode does' is wrong about middleware visibility.
surviving.recommendation: In the product, drop both private imports and the adapter-side validation. Route execution through the native handler with a per-call shim tool via ToolCallRequest.override (public; ToolNode supports dynamically supplied tools, tool_node.py:1388-1393), so ToolNode itself validates, builds the validation message, and formats the result. The remaining second validation is the inner tool.invoke(arguments) in DerivedToolSet; either document it or hand the shim's parsed arguments through. Add an import-time capability check that ends as ERROR, and test at both ends of the allowed langchain-core and langgraph-prebuilt ranges.
surviving.corrected_claim: The prototype depends on langchain_core's private _format_output (arci_langchain.py:37, called positionally at :214) and langgraph-prebuilt's unexported ToolInvocationError (:26, :192). FINDINGS.md:143 already discloses these as private/version-sensitive, but understates two things. (1) The planned pin langchain>=1.4,<2 (adr-0012-draft.md:22,30) constrains them only transitively (for 1.4.9: langchain-core 1.7.5..<2.0.0, langgraph-prebuilt 1.1.0..<1.2.0, and later langchain 1.x may move those). Removal or rename fails at import and already ends as ERROR, but a call-signature drift does not: a _format_output signature change raises TypeError after the body ran, inside user middleware, so ToolRetryMiddleware re-executes the body and ToolErrorMiddleware swallows it, with no harness latch (FAIL or a completed trial, never ERROR); a ToolInvocationError constructor change crashes in SerialOrder with zero bodies (FAIL/crash). (2) The SerialOrder pre-validation is not where native validates: native validates in the innermost execute and returns the error ToolMessage through user middleware (tool_node.py:964-1029), whereas the spike raises from the outermost wrapper (:1071-1088). Exception-catching middleware (the only kind check 3 tests) sees no difference, but any middleware that observes or rewrites returned messages diverges: natively it sees and can rewrite the validation error, under the spike it is never entered, so model-visible text can differ. The comment at arci_langchain.py:179 and the "identical native feedback" claim are therefore accurate only for the three tested policies. Both problems are avoidable with public API: have Boundary call handler(request.override(tool=shim)) where shim is a per-call StructuredTool with the original args_schema whose body calls boundary.call with the raw arguments, and remove validation from SerialOrder. In-memory probes show this equals native for bad arguments (including spy and rewrite middleware), dict and multi-line results, and preserves ToolFault propagation, retry recovery (1 body, 2 calls), multi-call ordering and budget exhaustion. The inner tool.invoke in DerivedToolSet (:86) remains a second validation; the product should document it, add an import-time capability check that ends as ERROR, and test both ends of the allowed langchain-core and langgraph-prebuilt ranges.

surviving.title: In-body unsupported shapes are recorded as agent-visible tool failures although an existing kernel path already latches harness_error; reject_unsupported is needed only outside a live tool call
surviving.claim: FINDINGS presents snapshot-raising as the only route available today. For rejections raised inside the registered tool callable (Command result, non-JSON result) that is not so: ToolBox already latches harness_error immediately when the callable raises a non-Exception BaseException or returns a non-JSON value. The spike raises a RuntimeError instead, which the kernel records as an ordinary tool error and raises to the agent as ToolFault, so user retry middleware re-runs the body and the ERROR depends on snapshot being reached.
surviving.recommendation: Make the adapter's rejection exception derive from BaseException (or return the offending value) for in-body rejections so the existing latch fires at once, survives a hang, and is neither recorded as a tool fault nor retried; this needs no kernel change. Keep ToolBox.reject_unsupported(detail) for the cases with no live tool call in progress: async detection, and every rejection in replay, including registration checks that run inside the agent function there (arci_langchain.py:248). Have it raise a non-Exception type so default retry/error middleware cannot catch it, keep details digit-free (format_diagnostic scrubs numbers), and note that in replay a leftover recording turns it into ERROR/replay_miss by latch precedence, which is still never FAIL.

surviving.title: Model-visible tool output is not native outside the two shapes check 8 tests: list-of-strings results and every real tool error differ
surviving.claim: FINDINGS.md row 8 (line 68) reports native message parity as OK, but run_spike.py:434-437 tests only a multi-line string and a dict. A tool returning a list of strings reaches the model as a content-block list instead of the JSON text native LangChain produces, and any real tool exception reaches user middleware as ToolFault with numbers and paths replaced by placeholders. Both happen in clean conditions, in both arms, so the gate would measure a different agent from the one in production; FINDINGS.md:103-108 mentions the error retyping only as 'can behave differently' and does not mention the list case at all.
surviving.recommendation: Before phase 3, extend the parity check to list results and to real-error text and type under a typed retry policy. For real (non-injected) errors the adapter runs in-process and already holds the original exception in DerivedToolSet._bind.execute (arci_langchain.py:83-93): keep it and re-raise it from the tool position after ToolBox has recorded the call, so type and message are native; only injected faults and replay need be ToolFault, and the recipe must say that injected faults do not match user retry_on filters unless the adapter raises a subclass that does. Fix the list case by letting ToolNode's own execute path format the result (see next finding) rather than calling the private formatter.
surviving.corrected_claim:
Check 8's OK (FINDINGS.md row 8) covers only a multi-line string and one dict, and there are two gaps behind it.

(a) Undisclosed: a tool returning a non-empty list of plain strings reaches the model as a content-block list (`['alpha','beta']`, `.text` = `'alphabeta'`) instead of native's JSON text `'["alpha", "beta"]'`. `Boundary` (arci_langchain.py:213-218) returns the private `_format_output` result from `wrap_tool_call`, and ToolNode does not apply `msg_content_output` (tool_node.py:317-344, 1475-1476) to a wrapper's return (tool_node.py:1061-1072). Twelve other shapes matched. This is a small fix, not a design change.

(b) Disclosed but understated: FINDINGS.md:103-108 already says real tool exceptions surface as ToolFault, that type-specific retry/error policies can behave differently, and that error details are scrubbed of numbers and paths. It does not say that the scrubbed, `ToolFault:`-prefixed text is model-visible through stock middleware, including the default `ToolRetryMiddleware()` message. It also does not say that in the clean condition a typed `retry_on=(ValueError,)` policy turns a native recovery (2 bodies, `'forty-two'`) into an uncaught ToolFault crash FAIL (1 body). No spike check exercises error text or a type filter (probe_app.py:56-60, scripted_model.py:52).

Before phase 3, extend the parity check to list-of-string results and to error text and type under stock and typed retry policies, and move the error limit into the stated supported scope. The reviewer's proposed fix (re-raise the original exception live, ToolFault only for injection and replay) should not be adopted as stated: replay has only the normalised ToolFault, so a typed policy would retry live but not in replay, and the two would diverge. The product needs either a documented restriction (user policies must match ToolFault) or a design that behaves identically in live and replay.

surviving.title: The splice-your-middleware-between-ours API is unenforced: natural mistakes silently disable the user's retry policy or hang the trial, and a simpler API is feasible
surviving.claim: The user must write middleware[:1], theirs, middleware[1:] (user_app.py:32-36). Nothing checks the placement, and the two obvious alternatives a user would write both fail without a diagnostic. FINDINGS.md:150-151 says only that the two entries 'must remain outermost and innermost'. The burden inventory (FINDINGS.md:117-124) is also incomplete: the adapter hardcodes the agent input as json.dumps(task) (arci_langchain.py:252), so any real agent needs a task-to-input mapping the list omits, and the user_burden check (run_spike.py:540-563) writes a hardcoded list of names and cannot fail.
surviving.recommendation: Do not ship the splice. Minimum: the adapter composes the list itself (helper, or the adapter owns the create_agent call and takes the user's kwargs per arm), and SerialOrder turns a second entry for the same call id into a harness ERROR instead of waiting. Preferred: spike (b) properly with real injected faults and replay, since it removes the Boundary middleware, the private formatter and the hand-built validation error, and reduces the rule to 'ARCI middleware first'. Add an explicit task-to-input hook or convention (for example task['input']). Reword the plan objective (PLAN.md:41-42): this design is a small adapter module, not one changed line.

surviving.title: Recoverable agent behaviour and a mainstream create_agent feature end as harness ERROR, and neither is listed as a limit
surviving.claim: Check 7 exercises only the four shapes named in the brief, while the adapter has about fifteen reject reasons. Two of the untested ones matter for real models: a mis-named tool call, which native LangChain feeds back to the model as a recoverable error, and response_format structured output, which makes every trial ERROR. FINDINGS.md's scope list (lines 137-154) mentions neither.
surviving.recommendation: Pass unknown-tool calls through to the native handler (or to ToolBox, which already records them as a ToolFault) so a model's mistake is graded as agent behaviour, not excluded as a harness error; this matters for the phase 5 study on real models. Decide explicitly whether response_format is in scope for v2.0: either capture structured_response in the snapshot or name it in the recipe as rejected. In the product tests, cover every reject reason, not the four from the brief.
surviving.corrected_claim:
Check 7 exercises four of the adapter's 15 reject reasons (async, artifacts, return_direct, Command). Two untested ones turn ordinary agent behaviour into ERROR/harness_error, and neither FINDINGS.md:137-154 nor PLAN.md phase 3 lists them as limits.

1. A mis-named tool call. Native LangChain answers it with a recoverable error ToolMessage ("Error: look_up is not a valid tool, try one of [lookup].") and the run completes. The adapter rejects it as "unknown tool" (arci_langchain.py:182-184), even with user retry middleware present. The kernel itself classes an unknown tool as an agent-visible ToolFault(unknown_tool), not a harness fault (toolbox.py:288-296). Because any ERROR trial makes the whole experiment verdict ERROR (docs/STATISTICS.md:53), one hallucinated tool name from a real model voids the run rather than being excluded.

2. Tool-calling structured output: `response_format=ToolStrategy(...)`, or a raw schema on a model without provider-native structured output, which AutoStrategy converts to ToolStrategy. The model node ends on a ToolMessage, so `after_model` rejects with "non-AI model response" (lines 144-146) on every trial, and `structured_response` is never captured. `ProviderStrategy` is not rejected: the adapter captures the JSON text as final_output.

For the product: restoring native parity for unknown tools requires passing the call through to the native handler. Routing it to ToolBox would raise ToolFault and end FAIL/crash where native recovers. Product tests should cover every reject reason. The fix is local (two branches plus snapshot capture) rather than a change to the middleware architecture.
